item.description:
Hind Rajab Foundation urges Germany to arrest Israeli soldier over Gaza war crimes

The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) has urged Germany to arrest an Israeli soldier, Almog Keisi, who has been sighted in Luneburg this week, accusing him of war crimes, crimes against humanity and acts of genocide in Gaza.

In a statement, the foundation said it filed a criminal complaint with Germany’s Federal Public Prosecutor in Karlsruhe under the principle of universal jurisdiction set out in Section 1 of the German Code of Crimes against International Law that cover genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes.

German authorities can exercise jurisdiction over these offences regardless of the suspect’s nationality or where the alleged crimes were committed, the statement read.

HRF said that Keisi participated in the burning of residential buildings in Gaza City’s Sheikh Radwan neighbourhood between 9 and 10 October 2025, following the announcement of a ceasefire agreement and ahead of Israeli forces’ withdrawal from northern Gaza.

According to the complaint, Keisi posted photographs on 10 October showing himself placing explosives around civilian objects and later posing in front of buildings engulfed in flames. Other soldiers from the Givati Brigade also shared photographs of the burning structures, describing the destruction as a celebratory farewell.

HRF said it had geolocated the buildings near Al-Mawhobeen Secondary Female School and cited NASA fire-detection data and satellite imagery as corroborating evidence of the fires and damage.

Dyab Abou Jahjah, HRF’s general director, said: “Germany has received evidence against suspected war criminals before and chose to look away. Meanwhile, it arrests and prosecutes people for waving keffiyehs or chanting slogans against the genocide."

"So the question stands: how long will Germany spend its resources prosecuting those who fight the genocide instead of those who commit it?"

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Israeli occupation, Iranian interference threat to Lebanese sovereignty, Aoun says
item.description:
Israeli occupation, Iranian interference threat to Lebanese sovereignty, Aoun says

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has accused Iran of meddling in Lebanon's affairs through Hezbollah's weapons and also demanded Israel withdraw from the country's south.

In a speech on the eve of Lebanon's 83rd independence anniversary, Aoun vowed to press ahead with plans to bring all weapons under state control. 

Lebanon's sovereignty still faces two threats, he said: "The Israeli occupation of parts of our territory" and foreign interference from "influential elements within the Iranian regime" through weapons and decisions outside the authority of the Lebanese state. 

On Israel, Aoun stressed Lebanon's message was clear and direct: "Withdraw from every inch of Lebanese territory. Stop your attacks."

There would be "no occupation ever again", he said. "And no weapons outside the state that... serve the interests of, foreign powers," he added, without naming a specific group.

Such weapons may once have served a purpose, he said, but later imposed a high cost on Lebanon when they came to serve causes beyond its borders. 

"You must hand over your weapons," Aoun said.

The Lebanese government has committed to disarming Hezbollah, whose arsenal has long outstripped that of the national army and which has justified its weapons as necessary to resist Israel.

In June, Lebanon and Israel signed a framework agreement that included the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual Israeli withdrawal from territories it occupies in the south and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the area.

But implementation has stalled and Hezbollah has refused to surrender its weapons.

Israel's army still carries out strikes, shelling and detonations in the south, where its forces are operating in a self-declared "security zone" running around 10 kilometres.

Report by AFP

item.description:
Turkey says Israel could use Druze support to launch Syria operation

Israeli could use its support of the Druze to launch an operation in Syria, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said, warning that such an attack could lead to a wider conflict in the region.

In an interview with Turkish media, Fidan said Israel is providing military equipment and support to a Druze tribe in Syria, and may use that support to provoke the Syrian army and launch an attack.

Fidan said Turkey has discussed such the possibility of this operation with European and American officials.

The violence last year in Druze-majority Sweida - which began with clashes between Druze factions and Bedouin fighters in the southern province - left more than 2,000 people dead, including 789 Druze civilians, according to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] How Europe’s green hydrogen ambitions could keep Tunisia’s worst polluter alive
item.description:
How Europe’s green hydrogen ambitions could keep Tunisia’s worst polluter alive

Submitted by Francesco Torri on Tue, 11/17/2026 - 11:13
A German-backed plan sold as a clean energy transition is seen by many Tunisians as a lifeline for a heavily polluting phosphate industry
Smoke billows from the chimney of a section of the state-run phosphate processing plant in the southern city of Gabes on 31 October 2025 (Fethi Belaid/AFP)
Off

As Tunisia’s green hydrogen strategy is being promoted as a cornerstone of Europe’s clean energy transition, residents in the southern city of Gabes argue it could instead extend the life of one of the country’s most polluting industrial complexes while increasing pressure on scarce resources.

On 21 October 2025, around 100,000 people marched through Gabes in one of the largest environmental protests North Africa has seen in years. Demonstrators demanded the closure of the Groupe Chimique Tunisien (GCT), the state-owned phosphate complex that has polluted the city’s air and sea for decades.

Residents also mobilised against plans to decarbonise the GCT and turn it into a green hydrogen hub supplying Europe. Critics describe the project as a form of “green colonialism”, saying Tunisia would bear the environmental costs while Europe reaps most of the benefits.

Germany, which expects to import 50 to 70 percent of its hydrogen demand by 2030, has been the leading force behind Tunisia’s National Green Hydrogen Strategy, published in July 2024. Berlin financed the strategy and provided the technical expertise behind its design through GIZ’s H2Vert.TUN project.

As the strategy itself states, Tunisia aims to produce 8.3 million tonnes of green hydrogen annually by 2050. Of that total, only around 2 million tonnes would remain in the country. The strategy identifies the production of green ammonia at the GCT’s Gabes complex as the main and earliest domestic use planned for green hydrogen in Tunisia, while most of the remaining output would be exported to Europe.

Green hydrogen would replace the fossil hydrogen the GCT uses to produce ammonia for fertilisers and reduce its carbon emissions. But this “decarbonisation” would do nothing to address the plant’s other major sources of pollution, including sulphur dioxide, fluorides and phosphogypsum, which have contaminated the environment for decades and continue to make Gabes’ residents sick.

The hydrogen is expected to be exported to Europe through the EU-backed SoutH2 Corridor. In parallel, Brussels pledged €35.4m ($38.9m) for Tunisia’s renewable energy infrastructure, while agreements signed with energy multinationals envisaged €120bn in private investment.

Yet little progress has followed.

“Everybody is waiting for something to develop,” Edward Koenen, head of finance and sales at ABO Energy, one of the companies that signed a memorandum of understanding, told Middle East Eye.

“The Tunisian government said they are not that interested in constructing anything, because there is no market for green hydrogen.”

Officially, Tunis has not changed course. On 1 October, it reaffirmed its commitment to the SoutH2 pipeline project by signing the Algiers Ministerial Declaration, but nothing has progressed beyond paper.

As the high costs associated with green hydrogen have become clearer, what some analysts once described as Europe’s “hydrogen hype” has begun to fade. In September 2025, the International Energy Agency cut its 2030 forecast for low-emissions hydrogen production by a quarter.

No to ‘green facade’

However, according to Saber Ammar, a Tunisian activist and researcher at the Tunisian think tank Transnational Institute, there is another element behind Tunisia’s stall on its green hydrogen strategy: the opposition of Gabes’ residents and Tunisian civil society.

Opponents argue that the projects would primarily benefit European consumers while entrenching an industrial model that many residents of Gabes want dismantled.

“There was a coalition between the trade union, the social movement, the environmental justice movement, and we created some sort of an anti-green hydrogen front,” Saber told MEE.

‘Last year, starting from September, hundreds of people went to the hospital due to suffocation caused by the gases emitted by the industry’

- Islem Zrelli, member of Stop Pollution

One of the key components in this coalition is “Stop Pollution”, an environmental movement born in 2012 in Gabes to oppose the severe pollution and health impacts caused by the GCT.

Kheireddine Debia, one of Stop Pollution’s leaders, told MEE that what activists want "is to shut down the industrial complex, not to give it a green facade".

Debia received a six-month suspended sentence last month for protesting against the GCT, while nine other activists were handed prison terms of up to a year as part of a broader crackdown on dissent since President Kais Saied’s power grab in 2021.

Islem Zrelli, a young member of Stop Pollution, believes the GCT has already done too much damage. Last year’s protests erupted after more than 120 residents were hospitalised following severe gas leaks.

“Last year, starting from September, hundreds of people went to the hospital due to suffocation caused by the gases emitted by the industry,” he told MEE. “Many of them were kids and students from Chatt Essalem, my neighbourhood.”

Tunisia: Thousands protest in Gabes against chemical plant pollution
Read More »

The GCT’s phosphate processing and fertiliser production have caused long-term health problems among the population, including chronic respiratory illnesses. Its radioactive waste product, phosphogypsum, has been linked to higher cancer rates and has polluted the Gulf of Gabes, harming marine life and contaminating waters that residents rely on for their livelihoods and food.

In 2017, thanks to Stop Pollution’s mobilisation and civil society pressure, the government promised to dismantle the phosphate unit.

However, on 5 March 2025, a restricted ministerial council chaired by Prime Minister Kamel Maddouri reversed course. It removed phosphogypsum from Tunisia’s list of hazardous wastes, despite an estimated 70 million tonnes of the material having been dumped by the plant into the Mediterranean over the previous 25 years.

The controversial move is part of a 2025-2030 plan to expand phosphate production from under three million to 14 million tonnes a year. The council also approved the creation of pilot green ammonia units in Gabes, envisaged as the cornerstone of Tunisia’s domestic green hydrogen industry and a key component of the export-oriented hydrogen economy outlined in the German-backed national strategy.

For the people of Gabes, this means more phosphogypsum in the sea and higher emissions of toxic gases into the air, including ammonia, which a GCT audit found to be already exceeding permitted levels in 2025.

Green extractivism

Critics say Tunisia’s green hydrogen strategy could also carry significant social and economic costs.

“The problem is that green hydrogen needs fresh water, and Tunisia doesn’t have any fresh water,” Fadhel Kaboub, associate professor of economics at Denison University and president of the Global Institute for Sustainable Prosperity, told MEE. 

“So the solution is desalination, and desalination plants produce the salt brine, which is chemically toxic for sea life, that is dumped usually in the ocean. It kills the blue economy.”

‘It is reminiscent of the fossil fuel system. And with green hydrogen, we risk reproducing that model, with more foreign debt’

- Hanen Keskes, Greenpeace MENA

The worsening water stress that environmentalists have warned about for years has already become a reality in Tunisia. This year, the country faced its hottest summer on record, with power cuts that stopped the water pumps and left towns without water for days, prompting protests across the country.

According to the Transnational Institute’s analysis of the strategy, exporting six million tonnes of green hydrogen would also require more than 90 gigawatts of solar and wind capacity covering 500,000 hectares, about 3 percent of Tunisia and roughly twice the area of Greater Tunis.

Most of it would be concentrated in a planned “hydrogen valley” in southern Tunisia, much of it on communal land used by local communities for herding and small-scale farming. The strategy, however, offers few details on how such land would be secured.

Since 2016, Tunisia has loosened land laws to open agricultural and collective land to energy investors. In villages such as Segdoud, collective land has already been appropriated by the state for solar projects without compensation, according to residents and rights advocates.

Moreover, while the strategy promises more than 400,000 jobs by 2050, a 2021 study commissioned by GIZ warned that producing hydrogen with imported technology and exporting it as a raw material “would create limited jobs and value in Tunisia”. The study added that most of the jobs created would be temporary, tied to the construction of solar and wind projects.

Green hydrogen: The EU's new resource grab in North Africa
Read More »

Hamza Hamouchene, a founding member of the Environmental Justice North Africa (EJNA) network and programme coordinator at the Transnational Institute, argues that the strategy risks reproducing an extractivist economic model, where Europe profits from North Africa’s minimally processed resources while local communities see few lasting gains.

“Europe and its companies, what we call the Global North, want to continue to get their cheap natural resources, including green electricity and green hydrogen,” he told MEE. “Yet these projects end up not creating long-term, sustainable, good jobs for local populations.”

Officials estimate that producing every million tonnes of green hydrogen would require $25bn in investment, a cost they acknowledge Tunisia cannot bear alone. Critics warn that the strategy could lock the country into a new cycle of foreign debt, with public financing used to reduce risks for foreign investors.

“This is the built-in problem with extractivism, including green extractivism,” Hanen Keskes, political campaign lead at Greenpeace MENA, told MEE.

“You de-risk the European corporations through government loans, while just exporting raw, very depletable resources. It is reminiscent of the fossil fuel system. And with green hydrogen, we risk reproducing that model, with more foreign debt.”

Inside Tunisia
Achref Chibani
Jasper Humpert
Gabes, Tunisia

item.description:
Volunteers in black uniforms and body armour increasingly seen with figures such as Tommy Robinson

There is a worrying rise in “reckless and intimidating” vigilantes posing as security guards around far-right figures, security experts have said.

In recent months, uniformed figures wearing all black and body armour have been seen in the entourages of far-right figures including the convicted criminal Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, who goes by the name Tommy Robinson, and Paul Golding, the leader of the far-right political party Britain First.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] UAE condemns Iranian attack on Bahrain
item.description:
UAE condemns Iranian attack on Bahrain

The UAE has condemned the Iranian attacks on Bahrain as a “flagrant violation” of the Gulf state's sovereignty.

In a statement, Abu Dhabi reiterated “the UAE’s full solidarity with the sisterly kingdom of Bahrain and its support for all measures taken to safeguard its security and stability”.

Earlier on Sunday, Bahrain’s interior ministry said Iran attacked a civilian industrial facility near its capital, Manama. Iran said that the strike targeted air defence systems at two US military bases.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Burnham should ‘move on’ from Brexit, says Theresa May, as critics hit out over closer EU ties – UK politics live
item.description:
Issue dominates Sunday broadcast round following Friday’s deals on trade and youth mobility

  • Theresa May ‘aghast’ at Andy Burnham’s talk about rejoining EU

A chief concern for the Europeans as to the idea of the UK rejoining the bloc is frankly, the lack of British political stability this past decade, and the fear that a change in government down the line would lead to another backflip.

Burghart this morning went as far as saying that a future Tory government would reverse the deals secured on Friday.

We will certainly repeal this deal. This is a very bad deal.

I wish that Andy Burnham had chose not to reopen the Brexit issue. I think there was no need to do so.

And this deal will make a positive impact on both exports and imports, and crucially- this is the point that I noticed the retailers were making - it will reduce the costs that the retailers face, all of that Brexit red tape, millions of forms that they were having to fill in, frankly, pointlessly, as a result of the bad deals that we had.

If people think the status quo is really good on Brexit and that that’s been great for Britain, well, they won’t like this deal. I think most people think the status quo has been actually pretty rubbish. And we need to make it better and that is what this deal does.”
